questions.q: In Triton, what does one program instance (one value of `tl.program_id(0)`) usually process?
options: A whole block of elements, operated on as a vector
A single element, like a CUDA thread
One warp's worth of rows only
questions.why: Triton's unit of work is a block. The compiler decides how to spread the block across threads and warps.

questions.q: What does `offs = pid * BLOCK + tl.arange(0, BLOCK)` compute?
options: The element indices covered by this program instance
questions.why: `tl.arange` gives a vector 0..BLOCK-1, shifted by the block's start. Adding it to a base pointer gives a block of pointers.

questions.q: Why is a mask passed to `tl.load` and `tl.store`?
options: To select which GPU to use
The last block may extend past the end of the tensor, and masked lanes must not touch memory
questions.why: `mask = offs < n` disables out-of-range lanes. `tl.load` also takes `other=` to fill them, for example with 0 for sums or -inf for max.

questions.q: Why must `BLOCK` usually be declared as `tl.constexpr`?
options: It is stored in constant memory
It makes the value changeable inside the kernel
Block shapes must be known at compile time so the compiler can lay out registers and generate code
So it can be a float
questions.why: Each distinct constexpr value compiles a separate kernel. Block sizes in `tl.arange` must also be powers of two.

questions.q: What does a fused multiply-add kernel computing `x * y + z` save compared with two separate kernels?
options: One full write and read of the intermediate tensor from global memory
questions.why: Element-wise ops are memory-bound, so removing a round trip through global memory gives a large speedup.

questions.q: How is the launch grid usually specified for a 1-D Triton kernel?
options: As `(triton.cdiv(n, BLOCK),)`, often through a lambda over the meta-parameters
It is inferred from the tensor automatically
As the total number of threads
questions.why: A lambda such as `lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n, meta['BLOCK']),)` lets autotuning change BLOCK without recomputing the grid by hand.

questions.q: How does SiLU relate to sigmoid?
questions.why: It is smooth, non-monotonic for negative x, and is the gate used in SwiGLU.

questions.q: What is the tanh approximation of GELU?
questions.why: Exact GELU uses the normal CDF via erf. The tanh form was used in GPT-2 and is cheap to compute.

questions.q: How does a Triton kernel reduce a loaded block to one number?
options: With `tl.sum(x, axis=0)` (or `tl.max`, `tl.min`), which the compiler lowers to warp and shared-memory reductions
With a Python for loop over elements
questions.why: The cross-thread details are handled by the compiler. You still have to combine results across program instances.

questions.q: For a full-vector sum across many program instances, how are the partial sums combined?
options: Each program does `tl.atomic_add` into an output, or writes partials for a second pass
With a barrier across the grid
questions.why: Triton has no grid-wide synchronisation. Atomics are simple but not bitwise deterministic.

questions.q: In a masked max reduction, what should `other=` be for out-of-range lanes?
questions.why: Zero would win whenever every real value is negative. NaN would poison the result.

questions.q: Why can a row-wise softmax be done in a single program per row when the row fits in one block?
options: Triton caches the row in global memory
The whole row is loaded once; max, exponentials, sum and division all happen on-chip before one store
questions.why: This reads and writes the row once, against three or more passes for an unfused version.

questions.q: Why subtract the row max before exponentiating in softmax?
options: To make the output sum to 1
It changes the probabilities slightly but improves training
To keep every exponent ≤ 0 so exp can't overflow; the result is mathematically unchanged
questions.why: $e^{z_i - m}/\sum_j e^{z_j - m} = e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$. In float32, $e^{89}$ already overflows.

questions.q: What does row-wise logsumexp return?
questions.why: It is a smooth maximum, and it is what cross-entropy and attention normalisers need.

questions.q: A single-pass mean and variance kernel accumulates which quantities per block before merging?
options: Count, mean and the sum of squared deviations (M2), merged with Welford's formula
questions.why: Merging (n_a, μ_a, M2_a) with (n_b, μ_b, M2_b) uses δ = μ_b - μ_a and M2 = M2_a + M2_b + δ²·n_a n_b/n.

questions.q: Rows are longer than the largest block you want to use. How does a row-wise reduction handle this?
options: Loop over the row in chunks inside the program, accumulating a running result
questions.why: For softmax this needs an online update: keep a running max and rescale the running sum when the max changes.

questions.q: In a Triton matmul, what does `tl.dot(a, b)` operate on?
options: Two 2-D blocks loaded from A and B, producing a tile of partial products (using tensor cores where possible)
Two full matrices in global memory
questions.why: The kernel loops over K, loads a BLOCK_M×BLOCK_K tile of A and a BLOCK_K×BLOCK_N tile of B, and accumulates `tl.dot` results.

questions.q: Why is the matmul accumulator usually float32 even for float16 inputs?
options: Summing many half-precision products in half precision loses accuracy
questions.why: Accumulate in float32 and cast once at the end when storing.

questions.q: What does `@triton.autotune` do?
options: Benchmarks a list of configurations (block sizes, num_warps, num_stages) and caches the fastest for each key
Changes the algorithm to a different one
questions.why: The `key` argument lists the shape arguments; a new key value triggers a fresh benchmark.

questions.q: What does `num_stages` control?
options: How many tiles are prefetched ahead in a software pipeline, overlapping loads with compute
questions.why: More stages hide memory latency but use more shared memory, which can reduce occupancy.

questions.q: How does a tiled transpose avoid uncoalesced writes?
options: It reads one element per program
Load a 2-D block with coalesced reads, transpose it in registers with `tl.trans`, and store it to the transposed location
It uses atomics for every write
questions.why: Both the load and store then touch contiguous memory along their fast axis.

questions.q: For GEMV (matrix times vector), why don't tensor cores help much?
options: Tensor cores can't handle vectors at all
The operation does only about one multiply-add per matrix element loaded, so it is memory-bound
questions.why: Its runtime is set by how fast A can be read. This is why decoding (batch 1) in LLM inference is memory-bound.

questions.q: What does a fused matmul + bias + ReLU kernel gain?
options: The bias add and ReLU are applied to the accumulator before the store, avoiding extra passes over the output
It removes the need for tiling
questions.why: Applying epilogue ops in registers is nearly free compared with writing and re-reading the output.

questions.q: Why do Triton matmul kernels often require block sizes of at least 16?
options: Smaller blocks are not powers of two
`tl.dot` maps to tensor-core instructions that work on tiles of at least 16 in each dimension
Global memory reads must be 16 bytes
questions.why: The minimum depends on the hardware and data type, but 16 is the usual floor for `tl.dot` shapes.

questions.q: In a LayerNorm forward kernel, what is typically saved for the backward pass?
options: The per-row mean and reciprocal standard deviation
questions.why: Saving two numbers per row lets backward recompute $\hat x$ cheaply instead of storing it.

questions.q: Why does RMSNorm need only one reduction instead of two?
options: It uses the mean of squares directly and doesn't subtract a mean
questions.why: LayerNorm needs the mean before the variance (or a Welford pass). RMSNorm needs only $\sum x^2$.

questions.q: In the LayerNorm backward pass, why are dW and db hard to compute efficiently?
options: They sum over all rows, so many programs contribute to the same parameter gradient
They depend on the learning rate
questions.why: Common approaches are atomics, or writing per-block partial sums and reducing them in a second kernel.

questions.q: What is the input gradient of LayerNorm (with $\hat x$, rstd and $g = dy \cdot w$)?
questions.why: The two mean terms come from differentiating through the row's mean and variance. Both are row reductions.

questions.q: In inverted dropout with p = 0.2, a kept activation of 1.0 becomes what?
questions.why: Kept values are divided by 1 - p = 0.8 so the expected value is unchanged and inference needs no scaling.

questions.q: How does Triton generate random numbers for a dropout mask?
options: It reads random numbers from host memory
It can't; masks must be passed in
`tl.rand(seed, offsets)`, a counter-based generator that gives the same value for the same seed and offset
questions.why: Because the mask is a function of (seed, offset), the backward pass can regenerate it instead of storing it.

questions.q: For mean-reduced cross-entropy over a batch, how should the division by batch size be handled in a fused kernel?
options: Divide each row's loss (or its gradient) by N, or sum per-row losses and divide once at the end
Ignore it; it doesn't affect gradients
questions.why: Forgetting the 1/N makes gradients scale with batch size. Rows with an ignore label should also be excluded from N.

questions.q: The gradient of softmax cross-entropy with respect to the logits is what?
questions.why: This simple form lets a fused kernel compute loss and gradient from the same on-chip values.

questions.q: What problem does online softmax solve?
options: It computes softmax over a row in chunks, rescaling the running sum whenever a larger max appears
It removes the need for exponentials
It approximates softmax with a polynomial
questions.why: With running max m and sum ℓ, a new chunk with max m' updates ℓ ← ℓ·e^{m - m'} + Σ e^{z - m'}.

questions.q: FlashAttention's forward pass avoids writing which tensor to global memory?
options: The T×T attention score and probability matrices
questions.why: It keeps a running max, running sum and output accumulator per query block. The per-row log-sum-exp is saved for backward.

questions.q: In FlashAttention, when the running max changes from m to m', what happens to the output accumulator?
options: It is divided by the new max
It is multiplied by $e^{m - m'}$ before the new block's contribution is added
questions.why: All earlier contributions used the old max, so they must be rescaled to the new reference to stay consistent.

questions.q: How does causal masking let FlashAttention skip work?
options: Key blocks entirely after the query block are never loaded, roughly halving the compute
It masks every element individually and computes everything
questions.why: Only the diagonal blocks need element-wise masking. The upper-right blocks are skipped entirely.

questions.q: Rotary position embedding rotates which pairs of values?
options: Whole vectors relative to each other
Pairs of dimensions within each query and key vector, by angles proportional to the position
The values, not the queries and keys
questions.why: Because the dot product of two rotated vectors depends only on the angle difference, scores depend on relative position.

questions.q: What does a KV-cache append kernel do at each decode step?
options: Recomputes keys for the whole sequence
Writes the new token's key and value vectors into the cache at the current position for each sequence
questions.why: With variable-length batches each sequence has its own write position, so the kernel needs per-sequence offsets.

questions.q: Why is attention during decoding (one query per sequence) memory-bound?
options: Each step reads the whole KV cache to do little arithmetic per value read
questions.why: Grouped-query attention, cache quantisation and paging reduce the bytes read per step.

questions.q: In a Triton SDPA kernel, why is the score matrix scaled by $1/\sqrt{d}$ before the softmax?
options: It isn't; scaling is applied after
To keep score variance near 1 so softmax doesn't saturate
questions.why: Folding the scale into Q (or using $\log_2 e/\sqrt d$ with `exp2`) is a common micro-optimisation.

questions.q: What does grouping program IDs ("super-grouping") in a matmul improve?
options: L2 cache reuse, by having consecutive programs compute nearby output tiles that share rows of A and columns of B
questions.why: Row-major program order sweeps a whole row of tiles, evicting B before it is reused. Grouping launches a compact block of tiles together.

questions.q: When does split-K help a matmul?
options: When M and N are small but K is large, so there are too few output tiles to fill the GPU
When accuracy must be bitwise deterministic
When the matrices are square and large
questions.why: Several programs each handle a slice of K for the same output tile, and their partials are summed with atomics or a second pass.

questions.q: What are block pointers (`tl.make_block_ptr`) useful for?
options: Describing a 2-D tile by shape, strides, offsets and order, so loads and advances are clearer and can use hardware tile copies
questions.why: `tl.advance` moves the tile along K. On newer GPUs this can lower to bulk asynchronous tile copies.

questions.q: What does vectorised loading achieve in a simple vector-add kernel?
options: It adds the vectors in a different order
It removes the need for a mask
Each thread loads several contiguous elements with wide memory instructions, using fewer instructions per byte
questions.why: Triton usually vectorises automatically when it can prove alignment and contiguity, for example with `tl.multiple_of` hints.

questions.q: How should a kernel be benchmarked fairly?
options: Warm up first, synchronise around timed runs, repeat many times and report a median or similar statistic
Include compilation time in every run
Time a single launch with the Python clock without synchronising
questions.why: `triton.testing.do_bench` handles warm-up, synchronisation and cache flushing.

questions.q: For a memory-bound kernel, what is the most useful performance metric?
options: Achieved bandwidth (bytes moved ÷ time) compared with the GPU's peak
questions.why: If a vector add reaches about 90% of peak bandwidth, there is little left to gain.

questions.q: Why might increasing `num_warps` slow down a kernel?
options: Each warp gets a smaller share of the block's work and registers, adding overhead or reducing per-thread reuse
More warps always speed things up
questions.why: The best value depends on block size and kernel type, which is why it is usually autotuned.

questions.q: What does the roofline model tell you about a kernel?
options: Whether its arithmetic intensity puts it under the bandwidth limit or the compute limit, and how far it is from that ceiling
questions.why: Plotting achieved FLOP/s against FLOPs per byte shows which resource to optimise for.
